name: Erythromycin topical
lead: Topical erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic applied to the skin, most commonly as a 2% solution, whose US-labelled indication is the topical treatment of acne vulgaris.[1] People use it to reduce inflamed pimples and clear breakouts so the skin looks calmer and less blemished. It acts against skin bacteria such as Propionibacterium acnes (now Cutibacterium acnes), and reviews of topical acne antimicrobials list erythromycin alongside clindamycin as commonly used agents.[2][5]

Beyond acne, small older reports have described erythromycin solution used with a topical corticosteroid in perioral dermatitis.[3] Its label lists local reactions such as peeling, dryness, itching, redness and oiliness, and warns that pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents.[1]

Erythromycin itself dates to 1952, when Eli Lilly isolated it from soil samples sent by the Filipino scientist Abelardo Aguilar.[6] Dermatology references note that widespread antibiotic use has raised rates of resistant acne bacteria, especially to macrolides such as topical erythromycin, so antibiotics are generally used as part of combination therapy.[5] Little looksmaxxing-community material was found for this entry; it appears in an appearance context because of acne.

paras: The US drug label for erythromycin topical solution 2% lists a single indication, the topical treatment of acne vulgaris.[1] A review of topical clindamycin describes topical antimicrobials as working partly by suppressing propionibacteria and partly through non-antimicrobial mechanisms, and names topical erythromycin among the commonly used agents.[2]

Wikipedia's acne article says clindamycin and erythromycin are commonly applied to the skin for mild to moderately severe acne, and that oral antibiotics are generally more effective than topical ones and resolve inflammatory lesions faster.[5] Erythromycin with benzoyl peroxide is listed as a combination product on the Wikipedia erythromycin page.[6]
A 1983 report in Cutis described six patients with perioral dermatitis treated with 1.5 percent erythromycin solution together with a tapered hydrocortisone valerate cream.[3]

sections.h: Why acne treatment matters for appearance
paras: Wikipedia reports that acne affected about 633 million people in 2015 and affects an estimated 80 to 90 percent of teenagers in Western countries, persisting into the twenties and thirties in nearly half of those affected. It estimates that scars affect 95 percent of people with acne vulgaris, with atrophic scars the most common type, and that dark marks after inflamed lesions can last months or years if untreated. It also notes acne can reduce confidence and self-esteem.[5] Treating inflammatory lesions early is the context in which topical antibiotics are discussed.

Erythromycin is bacteriostatic: it binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation of tRNA, halting protein synthesis. Wikipedia reports the drug (C37H67NO13) was first totally synthesised by Robert Burns Woodward's group, published in 1981, and that oral erythromycin is metabolised by CYP3A4.[6] These systemic details concern oral dosing; topical solutions are applied to the skin surface.

Reviews of topical acne antimicrobials describe suppression of propionibacterial growth together with non-antimicrobial effects.[2] A registered Phase 4 trial is comparing the anti-inflammatory effects of topical erythromycin and clindamycin in acne patients.[4]

Wikipedia reports that Abelardo B. Aguilar sent soil samples from the Philippines to Eli Lilly and Company in 1952 and that Lilly isolated erythromycin from them, marketing it as Ilosone, named after Iloilo province. Lilly's patent was granted in 1953, and Aguilar received no further credit.[6]

Wikipedia notes that widespread overuse of antibiotics has raised rates of antibiotic-resistant C. acnes worldwide, especially to tetracyclines and macrolides, with topical erythromycin given as the macrolide example. Because of this, dermatologists prefer antibiotics as part of combination therapy rather than alone, and benzoyl peroxide, which does not appear to generate resistance, is used alongside them.[5]

The label reports occasional local reactions including peeling, dryness, itching, erythema and oiliness, as well as eye irritation and skin tenderness; generalized urticarial reactions requiring systemic steroids have also been reported.[1]

The label carries a warning that pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, and notes there are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women, advising use in pregnancy only if clearly needed. It adds that erythromycin has been reported to cross the placenta, with generally low fetal plasma levels.[1]

A review of topical clindamycin in acne reported that clindamycin appears superior in efficacy to some other options, and treats erythromycin as one of several accepted topical antimicrobials.[2] A 1983 case series of six perioral dermatitis patients reported success with erythromycin solution plus hydrocortisone valerate; it was not a controlled trial.[3]
A Phase 4 trial comparing the anti-inflammatory effects of topical erythromycin and clindamycin in acne patients (30 participants) is registered as recruiting.[4]

timeline.event: Eli Lilly isolates erythromycin from Philippine soil samples and launches it as Ilosone.[6]
Robert Burns Woodward's total synthesis of erythromycin is published.[6]
Cutis report of erythromycin solution with hydrocortisone valerate in six perioral dermatitis patients.[3]

lore.intro: Topical erythromycin is mentioned only occasionally in the T Nation forum, in acne threads.[7]

claims.claim: A course of prescribed topical erythromycin can clear lingering acne.
claims.believers: One T Nation member said a doctor gave him topical erythromycin for acne that lingered on his back for about eight months after a hormone cycle, and it cleared within a month.[7]
claims.experts: The US label lists acne vulgaris as the indication and acne reviews describe topical antimicrobials as commonly used agents; clinical references note resistance concerns with macrolides.[1][2][5]

card.summary: Old-school topical macrolide antibiotic for acne, labelled for that use only.
card.note: Prescription antibiotic; label warns of local irritation and rare colitis reports.

quick.overview:
Topical erythromycin is a prescription antibiotic solution applied to the skin for acne. The US label lists acne vulgaris as its indication.

Reviews of acne treatment include it among the commonly used topical antimicrobials, next to clindamycin.
quick.mechanism: It is an antibiotic that suppresses acne-associated skin bacteria; reviews also describe non-antimicrobial effects of topical antimicrobials generally.
quick.risks: The label lists dryness, peeling, itching, redness and oiliness, and warns that colitis has been reported with antibacterials generally. Pregnancy data in humans are inadequate.

chain: Fewer inflamed pimples and clearer-looking skin over weeks
angle.text: Topical erythromycin is a prescription treatment for acne, aimed at the inflamed spots that make skin look blemished. Acne medications in general take roughly eight to twelve weeks to show their effect, according to a Wikipedia summary of acne treatment.[5]
